title: Teach us to pray (Luke 11:1–4)
hook: Luke's shorter version of the Lord's Prayer

segments.voice: Yesterday, Martha in the kitchen and Mary at his feet. Your line was one thing is needful. Did you manage to sit before you served? Day five hundred forty-three.

Luke keeps showing Jesus at prayer: at his baptism, all night before choosing the twelve, on the mountain when his face changed. Today it happens again. He is praying in a certain place, and his friends wait nearby until he finishes. They stand a little way off and watch. When he stops, one of them asks a question. Not about miracles, not about the kingdom, not about who's the greatest. Just this: show us how.

In the King James Bible, the disciple says: "Lord, teach us to pray, as John also taught his disciples." John the Baptist had taught his followers to pray, Luke says. Now they want to be taught too. And what Jesus gives is short. The King James text of Luke reads much like Matthew's; some modern Bibles print Luke's version shorter still, opening with one word, Father, and then five requests. Hallowed be thy name. Thy kingdom come. Bread for each day. Forgiveness. And protection from the time of trial. That's it. Two small differences from Matthew are worth hearing. Luke's bread line in the King James is "Give us day by day our daily bread." Day by day: not a stockpile, a habit. And where Matthew says debts, Luke says: "And forgive us our sins; for we also forgive every one that is indebted to us." Sins for what we've done, debts for what others owe us. Matthew uses debts for both. One more surprise: the closing line, for thine is the kingdom, and the power, and the glory, isn't in Luke at all, even in the King James. The King James has it in Matthew. Some churches say it straight after the prayer; in the Catholic Mass it comes a moment later, after another short prayer by the priest. So a prayer said in churches today began as a short answer to a simple request. Teach us.
screen: then, large: `LORD, TEACH US TO PRAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray Luke's version, slowly. Settle and breathe. If you pray, you can say the King James lines one per breath, leaving long gaps: Hallowed be thy name. Thy kingdom come. Give us day by day our daily bread. And forgive us our sins; for we also forgive every one that is indebted to us. And lead us not into temptation. If you don't pray, take just one of those five requests and sit with it. Which one names something you actually need today? Bread, forgiveness, protection? Let it stay with you until the bell. The bell holds the time.
Father. The one word Luke's shorter version of the Lord's Prayer opens with, a disciple's request after watching Jesus pray, answered with just five requests after it.
Your line: teach us. Today, ask someone to show you one thing they do well, and listen like a student. Day five hundred forty-three.

howItsDone: Christians say the Lord's Prayer in worship and at home, usually in Matthew's wording; some churches add the closing doxology straight after it, while the Catholic Mass places it after a short prayer by the priest.

fork.setup: you've just watched Jesus pray in a quiet place. he finishes and looks up. what do you ask?
options: nothing. you wait for him to speak.
fork.reveal: one disciple asks: "Lord, teach us to pray, as John also taught his disciples." the answer is a short prayer, not a lecture.

original.note: Greek: Father, spoken to God directly. some modern Bibles open Luke's prayer with this one word.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Lord's Prayer is the same everywhere in the Bible.
what it means: Luke gives a short prayer as Jesus' answer to a disciple's request.
what a scholar hears: Luke's line asks forgiveness for "sins" and forgives those "indebted" to us, where Matthew's says debts both times.

notes: Shorter text of Luke 11:2–4 in older manuscripts (e.g. P75, Sinaiticus, Vaticanus) vs the longer Textus Receptus behind the KJV. Stated generally. Confirm.
The doxology is absent from Luke and from the earliest manuscripts of Matthew; Catholic Mass places it after the embolism. Confirm wording.
'Teachers often gave their followers a prayer of their own': inferred from Luke 11:1; framed carefully. Confirm.
Practice invites saying real KJV lines from Luke 11:2–4, offered as 'if you pray'. The phrase 'protection from the time of trial' paraphrases 'lead us not into temptation'.
